#4760. Tesla to end Cybertruck production as sales stall at ~10% of plan

Tesla is ending Cybertruck production. CEO Elon Musk announced early Friday that the automaker will “wind down” the electric pickup at Gigafactory Texas around the middle of 2027, about three and a half years after the first deliveries.

Musk says it’s to make room for more Cybercab production. But Giga Texas isn’t short on space. The Cybertruck is short on buyers, and it sells at roughly a tenth of the 250,000 units a year Tesla built its line for.

Tesla will be winding down production of the Cybertruck at Gigafactory Texas around the middle of next year to make room for increased Cybercab production

That’s all he said. Nothing yet on how long Tesla will keep selling inventory or what happens to parts and service for existing owners.

Tesla doesn’t break out Cybertruck deliveries. It lumps them into “Other Models,” along with the Model S, Model X, and now the Semi.

That bucket tells the story anyway. Tesla delivered 8,295 “Other Models” in Q3 2026, down 48% year-over-year and the lowest since Q2 2021. With Model S and Model X production over since April, we estimated that 7,000 to 8,000 of those were Cybertrucks.

That’s a pace of about 30,000 trucks a year. Tesla planned the Cybertruck line for 250,000 units annually, and its latest shareholder letter still lists more than 125,000 units of installed capacity. So the truck is selling at about 12% of plan, and roughly a quarter of what’s actually installed.

The US numbers from Cox Automotive are worse. Cox estimates 3,519 Cybertruck sales in Q1 2026 and 3,744 in Q2, down from 14,416 in Q3 2024.

And not all of those were real customers. S&P Global Mobility data showed SpaceX bought 1,279 Cybertrucks in Q4 2025, and Musk’s companies took 1,339 in total, about 19% of US registrations that quarter. If it wasn’t for Musk’s self-dealing, the Cybertruck would probably be dead already.

Tesla tried to fix demand. It launched a cheaper rear-wheel-drive version in 2025 and pulled it months later, then brought a cheaper dual-motor trim to customers this summer. And then it raised prices by $5,000 in August. The dual-motor now starts at $74,990.

The “make room” explanation doesn’t hold up. Giga Texas has more than 10 million square feet of factory floor, by Tesla’s own count, and the Cybertruck line is already running at about a quarter of its installed capacity. Most of it is sitting idle.

The Cybercab also isn’t at a volume where it’s fighting anyone for floor space. Texas had 463 Cybercabs registered as of late October, and Tesla built a separate line for its “unboxed” manufacturing process.

If Tesla needs more Cybercab capacity down the road, it has the space. What it doesn’t want is to keep paying for a truck with its own stainless steel body, its own castings, and its own supply chain at 30,000 units a year.

Let’s call this what it is. Tesla isn’t ending the Cybertruck because the Cybercab needs room. It’s ending it because nobody’s buying it at anything close to the volume Tesla planned, and supporting a low-volume vehicle this unique is expensive.

I wouldn’t be surprised if Tesla lost a couple of billions on the Cybertruck experiment. Between R&D, pushing suppliers to produce 250,000 trucks per year, and deploying its own production line capable of 125,000 trucks per year, Tesla has invested billions. And with only ~70,000 trucks delivered in roughly 3 years, it probably never made any positive cash flow from the program.

They are just in-between growth phases. No need to panic just because they have discontinued three vehicles and the last successful vehicle they launched was the Model Y in early 2020.

The Cybercab line gives Musk a forward-looking reason to wrap a product failure in. Tesla did the same thing when it ended Model S and Model X production this year to free up Fremont for Optimus. It’s a lot easier to say “we need room for the future” than “this didn’t sell.”

We’ve said it many times: the Cybertruck is genuinely impressive to drive. Steer-by-wire and rear-wheel steering are real engineering, and nobody else has put them in a production pickup. But Tesla built a 250,000-unit factory for a polarizing $75,000+ truck that can’t be sold in Europe or most right-hand-drive markets. It just cancelled it for Australia and New Zealand two weeks ago. The math was never going to work.

It’s truly a sign of Tesla today. Musk used to talk about having a more traditional electric truck design if Cybertruck fails, but I doubt we will see that. Again, Elon is betting the house on autonomy.

#4759. CoinShares sells all treasury ETH, halves SOL holdings for buybacks

The October sales raised $19.3 million, nearly half the $40 million CoinShares can spend on buybacks before its next annual meeting.

European digital asset manager CoinShares sold its entire Ether treasury position and half of its Solana treasury holdings in October, raising $19.3 million to fund share buybacks.

CoinShares raised $16.6 million from the Ether sale and $2.7 million from the Solana sale, the company said in its third-quarter results on Wednesday.

CoinShares reported treasury holdings of 6,562 Ether (ETH) at a fair value of $17.6 million and 50,213 Solana (SOL) valued at $5.9 million as of Sept. 30. The company also held 235 Bitcoin (BTC) worth $19.6 million at quarter-end.

CoinShares’ board approved up to $40 million in buybacks on Oct. 22 under a five-year authorization that shareholders granted in September. The authorization covers up to 32.9 million shares, or 25% of shares outstanding. The $40 million program runs until the company’s next annual meeting, expected in the second quarter of 2027.

“That’s nearly half of the $40 million authorized by the Board and gives us the flexibility to act when conditions allow,” said Jean-Marie Mognetti, co-founder, president and CEO of CoinShares, referring to the sale proceeds in a Wednesday press release.

CoinShares also reported $7.4 billion in total assets under management, up from $5.5 billion at the end of June, driven by rising crypto prices and $125 million in net inflows during the quarter. Revenue fell 45% from a year earlier to $27.7 million, including $19.1 million in asset management fees.

CoinShares’ shares fell 5.41% to close at $3.15 on Tuesday, ahead of the earnings report, leaving them down 63% from their $8.61 close on the company’s April 1 Nasdaq debut.

#4757. Danielle Frankel Reimagines the 21st Century Bridal Store

After nearly 10 years in business, fashion designer Danielle Frankel Hirsch has opened a 12,000-square-foot location in Tribeca with interiors set to change the bridal game. To create the new space, which opened in early November, Frankel Hirsch worked with AD PRO Directory designer Augusta Hoffman and Studio Partners Architecture.

The nearly two-year design process is complete, and the Danielle Frankel bridal salon is now ready for appointments. “We’re finally at the point where my heart and my head have been,” says Frankel Hirsch, who worked with Hoffman on her previous Los Angeles boutique and New York City atelier. “Because this is our third space together, we can almost speak in shorthand now.”

Frankel Hirsch on the staircase wearing a shirt she designed from Fortuny fabric. Hoffman used the same Fortuny print throughout the space for wrapping side tables, keepsake boxes on the shelves, as well as for the woven seats on barstools.

The unassuming entrance to Danielle Frankel on Hudson Street

In the reception room just inside the street entrance, the desk is custom, the chairs are antique, and the custom pendant is by Jamb.

Hoffman worked with the artist Miriam Ellner to create eglomise paneling surrounding the staircase. “The eglomise is one of my favorite things because when we were working with the artist we worked so intimately with her,” Frankel Hirsch says. “We worked on the placement the way that we do our laces. We kept going back and forth with the drawings because I wanted it to feel like our lace placement.”

On a recent morning, a bride and her wedding party were busy in the VIP suite making a final selection. The beaming group entered the space through an unassuming brown storefront entrance on Harrison Street, its two large glass windows encased in a sheer linen. From there they ascended a staircase up to a large gallery with over 30-foot floor-to-ceiling windows overlooking the streets below on two sides, and a hand-painted mural pattern above on the ceiling.

The interiors of the original 19th-century Queen Anne–style red brick building were transformed by Hoffman (full disclosure: I am writing Hoffman’s design monograph publishing with Rizzoli in Fall 2027) into a modern, elegant bridal boutique that honors the history of the original New York Mercantile Exchange, first established in the 1880s to keep the standards of the grocer business. “We wanted the space to stay pretty bright and focus on the architecture, but we needed a lot of seating,” Hoffman says. “There was a lot of pressure because we wanted it to feel like Danielle and we wanted to leave our mark on the space, but it’s also so beautiful as is and we didn’t want to have too many interventions that take away from that.”

The rug, vintage Dutch leather armchairs, and custom clothing racks create one of the four seated zones in the gallery area. The wall features antique mottled glass windows. “We wanted this wall to feel historically accurate,” Hoffman says.

The custom oak screen features shelves for displaying miniature gowns by Danielle Frankel. The shelves are lined in silver leaf. The antique stool is reupholstered in a Fortuny fabric.

The view of the gallery area from a second floor bridal suite. The vintage teak seating set is reupholstered in a fabric by Manuel Canovas and the glass cocktail tables and Fortuny wrapped side tables are custom. The custom window panels are by Augusta Hoffman Studio for Wovn Home and the custom curtain hardware are bronze leaves designed by Hoffman. Hoffman pulled the leaf design from the details on the columns.

What previously functioned as a large, open space with a small mezzanine, had little existing infrastructure–no electrical, HVAC, or plumbing—and is now an area where brides can plot as they make the most important decision for their wedding day. In the gallery, Hoffman created distinct zones where wedding parties wait before their appointment in a private fitting room.

Much of the furniture was sourced by Hoffman and Frankel Hirsch together on trips to Paris. Antique glass vitrines separate the space, which they included from the previous New York gallery and filled with Frankel Hirsch’s own family wedding photos as well as printed details brides can use for their fitting. One vitrine has a board layered with references of crinoline and interlining. Another has custom Danielle Frankel cufflinks. An oak folding screen lines one half of the room, with miniature gowns set on shelves lined in silver leaf paper. Custom parchment and cerused oak racks Hoffman designed to withstand the weight of a wedding dress line the floor displaying roughly 65 dresses from Danielle Frankel collections.

The reflection of the wall is seen in the mirrored structure designed to house the elevator bank and stairwell to the street entrance. A framed antique floral plaster relief is flanked with 1930s Italian wall sconces in patinated glass and metal.

The staircase and elevator bank within the mirrored structure. “We had to add the elevator for function and for code, and we were like ‘How do we take this existing architecture and put an elevator in the middle of the room?’” Hoffman says. “It feels super unexpected, versus trying to hide it, and you get to see more of the surrounding architecture and light in the reflection.”

The custom rug is topped with an antique stool upholstered in a Fortuny fabric, a 1950s chair, and a 19th-century English pine console table.

The view from the sitting area adjacent to a bar. The vintage teak seating set was among the first items Hoffman and Frankel Hirsch sourced for the space. The custom bar stool is woven with a Fortuny fabric.

The view from within the staircase to the gallery area. The custom center table is by Rafael Carneiro Triboli and the French chairs are from the 1930s.

Hoffman and Studio Partners Architects took what was formerly the mezzanine, originally separated from the below with only a single-bar metal railing, and made it into a full wall with antiqued mottled glass windows. In the center they constructed a cascading grand staircase, cleverly concealing the stockroom underneath, which leads upstairs to three private bridal suites. The hallways, painted in Wenge by Benjamin Moore, lead to the bridal suites, each designed differently and filled with antique and vintage furniture, custom carpets, lighting, and racks. The walls are painted in Presidente Roman Clay by Portola Paints, an earthy contrast to the white and ivory dresses, which are naturally the center of attention for visitors in each room.

When guests are finished in their suites, there’s a bar in the gallery space where wedding parties can sit and make the final selection. The wedding party that morning had selected the dress and were toasting champagne to celebrate. “It’s just as much about the hospitality and the warmth as it is about the gowns,” Frankel Hirsch says.

In the VIP bridal suite, which can be accessed through a discreet entrance on Harrison Street, the custom sofa is upholstered in Holland & Sherry’s Corbel in Henna. The artwork features fragments of 19th century Japanese brocade.

The midcentury armchairs are upholstered in a Watts 1874 fabric and flank a vintage oak table.

The rack, mirror, and ceiling pendant are all custom in the VIP bridal suite.

In the dressing area of the VIP bridal suite, the ceiling pendant is custom and the closet wall covering is by Watts 1874.

The 1930s lounge chair is reupholstered in a Fortuny fabric and the 1970s lamp is from Brazil.

#4756. BYD’s electric hypercar hits 312 mph, first production car over 500 km/h

BYD’s Yangwang U9 Xtreme just reached 503.17 km/h (312.66 mph) on a closed highway in Abu Dhabi, making it the first production car ever to go faster than 500 km/h.

The FIA and Guinness World Records both recognized the run. It’s the all-electric hypercar’s second top-speed record in just over a year, and the one it broke was its own.

BYD announced the record on X this morning, saying the U9 Xtreme “has done the impossible” and calling it “the fastest production car on the planet.”

Abu Dhabi closed a 10 km section of the Sheikh Khalifa Bin Zayed International Road (E11), in the emirate’s Al Dhafra Region, for the attempt. That gave the team a 7 km straight. Marc Basseng, the German racing driver who set the car’s previous record, was behind the wheel again.

It took two days. Basseng maxed out at 490 km/h on the first day, per the FIA. After an overnight round of changes to the rear wing, damping, and tire pressures, he got to 503.17 km/h on his second attempt of November 1.

The previous mark was 496.22 km/h (308 mph), set at Germany’s ATP Papenburg proving ground in September 2025. That run had already pushed the Bugatti Chiron Super Sport 300+ and its 490.48 km/h from 2019 off the top of the list.

And it comes just days after BYD released footage of a U9 Xtreme crashing into a guardrail at about 280 mph during an earlier high-speed test. The driver walked away unharmed. BYD went right back out and hit 457.89 km/h on the next run.

The U9 Xtreme is the track-focused version of the Yangwang U9, the flagship supercar from BYD’s luxury brand. It uses four electric motors, each rated at 555 kW and spinning up to 30,000 rpm, for 2,220 kW combined. That’s over 3,000 PS, or nearly 3,000 hp.

It runs on a 1,200-volt architecture with a track-grade version of BYD’s Blade Battery. Those are LFP cells, the same chemistry BYD puts in its cheapest city cars.

For context, the Rimac Nevera R, which snagged a pile of EV world records last year, tops out at 431.45 km/h. The U9 Xtreme also holds the production EV lap record at the Nürburgring Nordschleife at 6:59.157.

Only 30 will be built, and BYD is charging around $3 million apiece. Don’t expect to see one in the US, where BYD doesn’t sell passenger cars.

The biggest one: this is a single-direction run. The two Guinness titles listed for the attempt, highest speed by a production car and by an electric production car, are both specified as “single direction.” BYD’s post claims four Guinness records, but the FIA’s announcement only lists those two for this run.

Production car top speed records have traditionally been the average of two runs in opposite directions, within an hour, to cancel out wind and road grade. That’s how Koenigsegg got its 447.19 km/h record with the Agera RS in 2017.

Bugatti took heat for exactly this in 2019, when the Chiron hit 490 km/h one way on a pre-production car. Bugatti itself said it wasn’t an official record.

The car also ran on bespoke semi-slick tires developed with Giti Tire. It’s not clear whether the 30 customer cars will get them.

A Chinese automaker best known for $10,000 city cars now builds the fastest production car in the world, and it’s electric. Not long ago, the conventional wisdom was that EVs couldn’t sustain high top speeds because the battery and motors would overheat long before the car ran out of road. BYD just ran 503 km/h on LFP cells. LFP cells!

But we’d hold BYD to the same standard we held Bugatti to. A one-way run on a highway with a 7 km straight is a great demo, not a definitive record, but impressive nonetheless.

Roadster 2 will now never be a record holder. It simple can't compete with today's hypercars nevermind those in 2028 when we actually see one leave a factory. Although with Tesla's record, it's usually 4 years from demo to production so that makes it 2030 for the Roadster 2.

And either way, let’s be honest: this is about marketing. Nobody is going to drive one of these 30 cars at 500 km/h. But it works. It’s a halo for Yangwang ahead of its new ultra-luxury sedan and for BYD’s push into Europe, and it makes the “Chinese cars are cheap copies” crowd look out of date.

Meanwhile, Tesla promised a Roadster that would hit over 250 mph back in 2017. Nine years later, it’s still not in production.

The real question now is whether Bugatti or Koenigsegg answers with a two-way 500 km/h run. Koenigsegg says its Jesko Absolut can theoretically do it, but it has never attempted a run. Is BYD what finally makes them try?

#4754. ‘Dune: Part Three’: An Exclusive First Look at the Sets

Nothing about the cinematic language of Dune is small—director Denis Villeneuve’s film trilogy does span multiple planets, after all. But throughout his work on the movies, including the upcoming Dune: Part Three, production designer Patrice Vermette has made sure to stay focused on the little details.

“My approach has always been with symbolism and semiotics,” Vermette tells AD. “It is my philosophy of design, because for Denis, empty design cannot exist. Things need to have a purpose. Need to have a signification.”

In conversation with Vermette about the sci-fi epic, examples of that core tenet come up often. Carefully designed details imbue hidden meaning in each set, creating a captivating, immersive on-screen world that earned the designer an Oscar for his work in the first Dune. The trilogy’s latest installment, Dune: Part Three, which lands in theaters on December 18, expands on that ethos. And for the final film in the series, the sheer scale of the sets was larger. “It was our last chance working in that world,” Vermette says. “It’s like in a fireworks [display], it’s the end, it’s the bouquet final, it’s like, ‘alright, let’s do it!’”

Robert Pattinson as Scytale, with director Denis Villeneuve.

Over 450,000 square feet of interior stages and 475,000 square feet of backlots were used for scenes shot in Budapest alone, with each set typically taking 14 to 16 weeks to build. (Filming also took place in Abu Dhabi and Iceland.) Even the sandworms that slither through the titular dunes got grander this time around: Instead of the relatively small platforms that were used to film worm-riding sequences as in the previous films, the production team built a 300-foot-long by 65-foot-wide sandworm in the middle of the desert.

Like in Dune: Part Two, Vermette was challenged to create entirely new sets for this installment, which adapts Frank Herbert’s 1969 novel Dune Messiah. One of the new settings viewers can expect is Wallach IX, the home of the powerful and secretive Bene Gesserit sisterhood. Throughout their planet, Vermette incorporated stone etchings that resemble human cells seen through a microscope, referencing the Bene Gesserit’s breeding program that has gone on for millennia. Mother nature also informed the architecture. “When you arrive on the planet, the buildings are basically eggs of a spider, like crops of spider eggs as you find them in nature,” Vermette explains. “Ecology has always been a huge source of inspiration for me, and also for the storytelling it gives—you know, they’ve got their web across the universe, for the genealogy they create.”

Another new setting is the Veteran’s District, where the Fremen, the native inhabitants of the desert planet Arrakis, retire after fighting in the catastrophic holy war spurred by Paul Atreides, aka Muad’Dib (Timothée Chalamet). In the previous films, the Fremen lived in communal residences lined with hand-carved stone that recorded their history and culture. Returning from the battlefield, they find mass-produced housing units instead of the “green paradise” they were promised would await them. Made of ceramic instead of rock, with stamped-on rather than hand-carved markings, the Veteran’s District represents an artificial facsimile of their former homes. “And when you put all these units together, and you look at the rooftops, it’s there to represent sand dunes,” Vermette explains. “All these triangles align [to look like dunes], but it’s fake.”

Another circular doorway represents an all-seeing eye near the lush Imperial Gardens, which illustrate Paul’s extreme wealth and control of resources—including water—on the dry planet of Arrakis.

There is a green paradise on Arrakis, just not for the Fremen. Lush gardens grace the planet’s Imperial Palace, a massive inverted pyramid with a large circle cut out of it—a reimagined version of the all-seeing eye. “I got inspired by the title of the book, Messiah, and from the fact that Denis, just like Frank Herbert, wanted to make sure that Paul Atreides was not going to be seen as a hero, and it’s a tale of being cautious about messianic figures,” says Vermette. Similar representations of the all-seeing eye are found throughout the palace, sinisterly implying that Muad’Dib is always watching.

In actuality, Muad’Dib’s personal quarters are completely isolated from the rest of the palace. His wife, Irulan (Florence Pugh), must find her way through a twisting mass of hallways to reach him. “Basically, she’s walking into the psyche of Paul,” Vermette explains. “She goes into a void, and then it’s all these mazes of one’s mind.” When we get to the end of the maze, we see that Paul’s inner sanctum resembles a humble desert camp. Not unlike the Fremen, his dwelling has been reduced to an echo of what once was. He is “living as a recluse because he doesn’t trust anybody,” Vermette explains. “He wants to go back to a place where he felt the most comfortable, which was the desert. So he recreated that space.”

“Denis really wanted that set to be the golden cage of Irulan,” Vermette says of these private chambers. “She’s married to the emperor, but she’s not free at all, she’s a prisoner.” The window is shaped similar to an infinity symbol, but is covered in metal screens. “It’s like eternity, but eternity is blocked. It’s like a cage.”

The entrance to the maze within Muad’Dib’s inner sanctum. Vermette designed 40 maze wall panels that needed to be moved into various configurations to shoot the scene, which was filmed in less than a day. Eight people were each assigned a portion of the 12-foot-high panels and learned a choreography of sorts, quickly moving into each configuration until they could do each one in five minutes or less. “We rehearsed and rehearsed, just like dancers or musicians; they knew exactly where to fit their pieces” within the roughly 14,400-square-foot space, says Vermette.

On the planet Wallach IX, the office of Bene Gesserit Reverend Mother Mohaim features stone carvings inspired by human cells under a microscope.

The Imperial Palace throne room took 20 weeks to build. Behind Muad’Dib’s emerald throne, the windows are shielded with metal cast screens inspired by Montreal’s Saint-Ambrose Church, which was built in 1925 by architect Ernest Cormier.

The all-seeing eye is a repeating symbol Vermette inserted throughout the Imperial Palace, including a representation seen here as the circular entrance of Paul’s Keep.

The architecture of this Imperial Palace corridor has slanted walls to reflect a pyramid-shaped exterior and flying buttress support structures inspired by Gothic-style cathedrals.

#4753. Bitcoin Covenants Part 6: FE Covenants — Enforcing covenants through cryptographically restricted signing keys

FE covenants encode spending constraints into the signing key, so only transactions that satisfy a predefined condition can be signed.

This is Part 6 in the technical article series about Bitcoin covenants by Cointelegraph Research. To read the previous article, click here.

Changing Bitcoin’s consensus rules is not merely a technical process. It requires that the network’s node operators, miners, developers and economic actors coordinate around a change. This coordination is difficult to achieve, which is why Bitcoin’s base layer has gradually ossified.

Researchers have spent the last several years investigating whether covenant behavior could be enforced without touching consensus rules. In May 2024, Jeremy Rubin, the original author of the OP_CTV proposal (BIP-119), offered an answer in a paper titled FE’d Up Covenants. His design proposed using functional encryption (FE) to move the covenant out of Bitcoin Script and into the signing key.

In ordinary public-key cryptography, a private key can sign any message. In hypothetical FE-based covenants, signing would be restricted to a predefined set of valid transactions. Bitcoin nodes would verify the signature with OP_CHECKSIG exactly as they do today, obviating the need for a soft fork.

Functional encryption (FE) generalizes public-key encryption. In ordinary cryptographic schemes, a private key can be used to fully decrypt a ciphertext and arrive at the plaintext. In FE, a master secret is instead used to issue subsidiary functional keys, each of which reveals only one chosen function of the plaintext. The holder of the functional key for a function f and the ciphertext of a secret x can compute f(x) but never gets to reveal x as a plaintext message.

In the academic literature, FE was first formalized by Dan Boneh, Amit Sahai and Brent Waters in 2011. Constructions for arbitrary functions followed from 2013, with polynomial runtime but overheads far beyond the resources of current computing technology. Furthermore, their security rested on new, untested building blocks called multilinear maps. Only in 2021 did researchers develop constructions from well-founded cryptographic assumptions, which could in principle open the door to practical implementations of FE.

The f in an FE scheme can be any feasibly computable function. However, in Bitcoin covenant constructions, f is a signing function. Its output is a Bitcoin signature for a transaction tx. Because this signature depends on both a private key and the transaction that is being signed, it takes at least two inputs, which is why Rubin’s design uses multi-input FE. For a covenant that only permits a single spending transaction, akin to OP_CTV, two inputs suffice. General, expressive constructions take more arguments, as in Rubin’s f(k, tx, program, proof).

Crucially, f does not sign directly with the private key k that is supplied in an encrypted form. Instead, the function derives a new key pair by tweaking k with a hash of the covenant’s spending policy. Signatures produced by f are valid for the tweaked public key, not for the base public key P itself.

To enable FE-based covenants from these primitives, a setup authority is required. It generates a Bitcoin key pair (the private key k and the public key P) as well as an FE key pair (the master secret msk and the FE public key mpk). It publishes P, mpk, k encrypted to mpk, and the functional key for f, which it derives from msk. The setup authority then needs to be trusted to destroy k and msk. Otherwise, it could sign spends that violate the covenant. With this setup completed, an indefinite number of new covenants may be created.

Every covenant has its own dedicated key pair, obtained by tweaking (k, P) with the spending policy. The private key of this tweaked key pair exists only inside f and is never revealed. The public key can be derived from P by anyone who knows the hash of the desired spending policy. This way, covenant receiving addresses can be generated. In practice, the receiving address would commit to a 2-of-2 script that requires a signature from a key the user controls alongside the FE signature. This is to keep unauthorized parties from triggering a transaction permitted by the covenant.

To create an FE signature for a covenant spend, the signer takes a tx that conforms to the spending policy and encrypts it to mpk. Using the encrypted tx, together with the encrypted k and the functional key published by the authority, they can then evaluate f. The function f signs tx with k tweaked by the hash of the spending policy. A transaction that breaks the spending policy of the address that holds the coins could at best be signed for some other, differently tweaked public key that does not control the funds.The function f can also be designed to block such a signature outright.

The general version of FE-based covenants with f(k, tx, program, proof) is strictly more expressive than OP_CTV. The general function proposed by Rubin takes a program that checks a condition on the transaction at spend time, and a zero-knowledge proof that the program accepts the transaction.

This zero-knowledge proof facilitates the implementation of the FE scheme, but does not add to it conceptually. A single fixed f works either way. Without the proof, f would have to be a general interpreter that runs any given program on tx itself. Such an f is large and costly to evaluate under FE. With the proof, f only has to verify a succinct proof. This could make it possible to enforce arbitrarily complex covenants without the need for more complexity in f. The proof also lets a spending policy depend on data outside the transaction, such as the result of an off-chain computation.

Goldwasser et al. (2014) introduced multi-input FE and built it on indistinguishability obfuscation. Multi-input FE and obfuscation are known to imply one another. Ananth and Jain (2015) showed that even single-input FE for general circuits yields obfuscation once it is made compact. The cryptographic primitive this design needs is therefore at least as hard to build as so-called indistinguishability obfuscation itself. Implementations of this principle remain at toy scale.

Carmer, Malozemoff and Raykova (2017) needed 3.7 hours to obfuscate a 12-bit pseudorandom function, a toy circuit of about 62,000 gates with a 64-bit key, far smaller than ECDSA signing on 256-bit numbers. The obfuscated program took 120 GB of disk space, and an evaluation ran for 67 minutes with 128 GB of RAM. The cost of implementing such a scheme would fall on whoever produces the signature, not on Bitcoin nodes. The authors called this “still far from practical.”

Furthermore, FE schemes that are practical cover only narrow function classes, such as the inner products of Abdalla et al. (2015), and the type of ECDSA signing required for Bitcoin covenants is not among them. Rubin’s paper concedes this point and lists under-developed cryptography and the setup trust assumption among its downsides. CTV-style opcodes remain far more efficient in bytes and verification, but require a base-layer change.

In our next article, we turn to Un-FE’d Covenants, which Rubin proposed to approximate covenant behavior without relying on impractical FE schemes. It replaces FE with oracle signers bonded through BitVM. [alloc]init’s Bitcoin PIPEs began in 2024 as an FE design and moved in 2026 to witness encryption. This proposal will also be covered in a follow-up article.

#4752. Zoomlion says its new, 1,600 hp hybrid tractor is the world’s most powerful

Chinese equipment brand Zoomlion showed up to this week’s China International Agricultural Machinery Exhibition with a new ultra-high-horsepower hybrid tractor that sets a new benchmark, offering more than 1,600 hp while cutting back on both fuel and fumes.

Zoomlion calls its new 9DX hybrid tractor a radical rethink of what a modern ag unit can be, combining the all-day pulling power of a conventional diesel machine with the efficiency, accuracy, and instant torque benefits of electric drive. The company claims its hybrid setup can reducing fuel consumption, emissions, and deliver lower operating costs, without asking massive industrial farming operations to walk away from diesel entirely.

The tractor itself gets a headline-grabbing 1,600 hp Zoomlion 9DX features an 800V hybrid electric powertrain and continuously variable transmission that delivering a peak torque of 7,200 Nm (~5,300 lb-ft) of torque. Getting all that power to the ground is a four track tank-drive system riding on Zoomlion’s in-house developed 762 mm (~30 inch) wide tracks that are designed to distribute the tractor’s considerable weight for maximum traction and minimum soil compaction. What’s more, the high-traction treads can push the big machine to hit a maximum speed of 40 km/h across grades and slopes of up to 12 degrees.

The 9DX also gets a high-capacity hydraulic system capable of delivering 636 liters per minute of flow (~170 GPM), allowing it to work with some seriously heavy duty implements like ultra-wide seeders and variable-rate fertilizer applicators.

The Zoomlion 9DX was one of several new machines at this year’s exhibition, which hosted more than 3,000 exhibitors and vendors – but the big hp numbers all over the show made an even bigger impression, leading AGCO’s director of global electronic and electrical engineering, Nicolas Meunier, to tell Chinese State news agency Xinhua that the country had moved on from producing mostly low-horsepower tractors to building some seriously large machines.

There’s no official word on specs and batteries, but the company has developed an 800V modular battery pack system for its other equipment offerings that can scale from 140-800 kWh of capacity while other top-shelf Zoomlion tractors featuring an ag version of Cummins’ 15 liter turbodiesel.

The 9DX tops off what’s sure to be another record year for Zoomlion, which is coming off strong early export quarters shipping into Germany, Australia, and the United Arab Emirates (UAE).

#4751. Liebherr expands excavator range with new, 250-tonne electric model

It takes some seriously heavy equipment to make an ultra-class mining truck look little, but that’s exactly what German equipment giant Liebherr does best, and its newest, 250-tonne production excavator keeps that tradition alive – only this time, it’s electric.

Liebherr began converting its diesel-powered mining excavators to electric in limited numbers back in 2024, and electric power has proven to be effective – moving millions of tons of dirt while saving millions of dollars in fuel and maintenance costs. Now, the company is translating that testing experience into regular production practice with the launch of a new, all-electric machine. Meet the R 9300 G8-E.

Based on the proven R 9300 G8 platform, the new Liebherr R 9300 G8-E packs an 850 kW (~1,140 hp) electric drivetrain designed to IEC standards and supports 6-6.6 kV power supplies. The company says its electric setup offers customers the same hydraulic power and bucket capacity (1.8 tonnes/cubic meter, or ~1.5 short tons/cubic yard) as the diesel version.

All that electric power ships with advanced electronics and operator assistance systems designed to maximize both efficiency and safety while giving mine operators more data to work and plan with. Liebherr describes its take on ADAS thusly:

The R 9300 G8-E comes with Liebherr Power Efficiency – Hydraulic Control as standard, which adapts hydraulic power to suit the machine’s load profile, reducing overall engine load factor. Thanks to its Generation 8 electronic architecture, the R 9300 G8-E is compatible with a range of Liebherr’s IoMine technology products, including its range of excavator Assistance Systems, the semi-autonomous Bucket Filling Assistant, the Skyview vision system as well as the data visualisation tool, Data View. Customers also have the option of installing Liebherr’s autonomous cable reel solution onto the excavator to assist with cable management and support machine mobility on site.

Like its repowered cousins, the big electric excavator does seem to have on-board batteries, but is primarily driven and operated with grid power, reducing charging and re-charging concerns and enabling round-the-clock operations for as long as grid power holds.

Liebherr touts the benefits of new R 9300 G8-E’s quiet, emissions-free running throughout its official announcement, but doesn’t stop there. The company says its EV, which makes do with thousands of fewer moving parts in its drivetrain, can also reduce maintenance requirements and associated operating costs in certain applications and site conditions while improving workplace conditions for the people who work in and around the machine.

Operating electric machinery inside mines must be mindblowingly good. Location is quite fixed, so you can just lay a HV cable to the grid with a spool at the vehicle end for local mobility. No noise, no vibration, no dirty emissions that have to be ventilated out for you not to die, instant torque, massive power and less maintenance on top?

The electric drivetrain also reduces vibration inside the cab, improving operator comfort, limiting fatigue, and potentially contributing to a safer working environment.

#4749. 41 Best Gifts for Women on All Special Occasions (2026)

The best gifts for the women in your life are probably right under your nose. Consider the unique facets of their personality, their hobbies, and what lights them up. Is it watching countless episodes of Barefoot Contessa, dreaming about an upcoming trip to the Poconos, sampling every kind of Sephora mini, or curating a high-design interior vignette? No matter the answer, a great present should match their energy to ensure they end up with something that reflects their essence and also shows you’ve been paying attention.

We’ve compiled a curated list of gift ideas tailored to all sorts of interests to minimize the guesswork for birthdays, Mother’s Day, the holiday-gifting scramble, and every momentous occasion in between. Our picks run the gamut—from home decor gems and high-tech gadgets to skin-care gift sets and culinary staples—but are still selective enough to feel special during the big unboxing reveal.

Silk pillowcases not only do wonders for your skin and hair, but they also make your bedscape feel more luxurious. Gifting her a set is a guaranteed upgrade to her nighttime routine.

A special pair of champagne flutes to mark special occasions and milestones will become a treasured fixture in her barware collection. This cheerful duo features bubbly glass adornments that will pair perfectly with a bottle of her favorite bubbly.

Receiving any Le Creuset cookware is a win for anyone who feels most at home in the kitchen. This Dutch oven is a treat that will become a staple for home chefs, who can use to make endless roasts, stocks, casseroles, and more. So as long as you’re invited for dinner, it’s a win for you, too.

Author Lydia Davis is best known for very short stories, some of them a single sentence long, but her essays are where the reader can see how her mind works. This first volume gathers five decades of writing on reading, translating, Proust, early tourist photographs, and the city of Arles. Complete the gift by dropping her off at a café, where she can read it while people-watching and underlining passages. Don’t forget to buy her favorite coffee.

No gift guide would be complete without a cozy blanket, and we’re making a bid on this mohair one. The colorblocked number is comfortable enough to drape over her shoulders whether she’s snoozing or curled up with a book.

A tablecloth is a smart gift idea for the singular reason that it’s not something you’d really ever buy for yourself. It’s delightfully multiuse: covering the many drink rings on your walnut table, performing as a park blanket in a pinch, and—most importantly—giving your favorite gal a sense of cohesive calmness as she sets her table.

Whether or not she has the dreamy silverware to match, Sabre’s serving set with trendy burgundy handles will feel like a little luxury for plating cheese boards and opening bottles. Elegant and slightly retro, they’re versatile enough to accompany both bold and understated tabletop decorations.

Paper napkins are fine for any regular evening, but a hostess deserves a beautiful set of cloth linens. Borgo delle Tovaglie, the Italian linen house Valentina Muggia took over from her mother, makes these in soft-washed pure linen. The red colorway is embroidered with an ivory floral motif that makes even takeout look planned.

“Few things are so favored in my home as this tabletop lighter,” says shopping writer Julia Harrison. “I got it on a whim, and then found myself using it routinely every night.” Perfect for incense, candles, burning cursed love notes, or enjoying a cigarette on the fire escape. Don’t forget the butane.

For the minimalist coffee lover who can’t resist a little chrome, Louise Roe has just the cup-and-saucer set to slide under the tree.

Enza Fasano works in the Apulian pottery tradition of Grottaglie, a town in Puglia, Italy. Her Guido cup and saucer bring the relaxed sense of a Southern Italian breakfast table to an ordinary weekday morning. The jade glaze is a staff favorite, and the set mixes with the line’s other colors if she wants to build a collection. Nota bene: It’s dishwasher-safe.

One thing about many a woman: She loves a pitcher. Not necessarily for pouring lemonade, but for the concept that she could, should the occasion present itself. These thick glass styles from Il Buco Vita double as great vases, too, making them a great hostess gift. They also hold plenty of water for her guests at one of her routine dinner parties.

If getting in a chapter or two of her current book du jour before lights out is a must, she’ll find a new best friend in this little task lamp. The head is magnetized, so you can direct light in pretty much any direction you choose. The sage shade has a notably relaxing quality.

No one has ever been charmed by a cardboard Kleenex box, which is what makes this such a satisfying find. Todd Nickey and Amy Kehoe designed the handmade lacquer tissue box with James Lowther of the Lacquer Company for a collection drawn from antiques they’ve collected over the years. The cover, made in Vietnam, slips over most standard tissue boxes. In khaki and chocolate, it will look at home on a nightstand or vanity long after cold season ends.

The year’s best photo deserves better than her camera roll. For the Ornament, Framebridge prints a picture you upload and sets it in a tiny frame on a green velvet ribbon, with a hidden pocket on the back for a note, then ships it in a vintage-style matchbox. It’s small enough to be a stocking stuffer and sentimental enough to hold its own among the bigger Christmas gifts.

A pair of candleholders from design giant Herman Miller (of Eames fame) is among the most affordable ways to say: “I think you have great taste.” If you feel inclined, you could tuck in a couple of her favorite scented candles to complete the gift.

This text that was pivotal in contemporary color research will surely become a favorite in her own book collection. Both visually appealing and full of knowledge, it includes 348 color combinations design nerds (like us) can use in their next project.

Rated the best overall waffle towels, this 100% pima cotton towel set is tested and loved by the AD staff. Their Imabari Towel Certification verifies they’ve been through the rigorous Japanese testing process for qualities of absorbency, durability, and craftmanship. After using them for a year, senior shopping editor Nashia Baker says “biggest perk is how much softer the towels have gotten after too many washes to count.”

If she’s the type to plan an entire trip around a hotel’s wallpaper, a Cabana Magazine subscription delivers three issues a year, focused on travel told through photography, writing, and graphic design. She’ll want it on her coffee table year-round.

AD’s Australian Open Door star Troye Sivan developed (and named) this sophisticated rose fragrance in honor of his sister, and chances are good the sweet story will resonate with the beloved female in your life. Splashes of myrrh and sugar bring a slightly smoky aroma to the rose base, while geranium and poppy add grounding floral notes.

Sometimes the smallest luxuries are the most impactful. Prada’s Sabrina Carpenter–approved lip balm is a pocket-size indulgence that reacts to your lip’s natural pH to bring a customized shade of pink to your pucker.

A compact blush in eight variations of pink is a can’t-miss contender in the makeup category. It’s a perfect stocking stuffer, and Violet Grey is the sort of cult favorite that will reflect your thoughtful gifting research.

Treat the woman in desperate need of a spa day to Nerra’s deep-cleansing bath system, which combats dull and dry skin with ancient Mediterranean self-care philosophy.

She can still travel with all of her lotions and potions, but this time, she won’t have to check a bag just to bring that special moisturizer. Keep Your Cadence makes beautifully designed, TSA-approved toiletry cases and containers that all lock together with magnets for easy transporting.

With four-layer organic cotton construction, luxuriously deep pockets, and a roomy, unisex cut, Boll & Branch’s cozy Dream Robe delivers on the promise of its name.

Merit’s two-piece gift set pairs one of its Signature Lip Liners with a coordinating Flush Balm (an everyday go-to for Harrison). There are seven pairing options, including two new shades, Cassis and Rose. The gift is an easy win for anyone whose makeup bag holds about three things, all of them good.

The gift of consistently good hair days? Priceless. La Bonne Brosse’s best-selling boar bristle brush is an indulgence that turns an otherwise unremarkable hair tool into an extra-special daily treat. It’s one of the few luxury gifts she’ll use every single morning.

This roomy robe’s modern take on the Breton stripe comes in a warm brown called Cocoa. Made in Portugal from organic cotton, it features a hood, two patch pockets, and a matching belt. Harrison “reaches for it every night.”

Here, Laila Gohar reimagines the nougat comb in an egg shape with an elegant black tassel to boot. It also makes the perfect tool for a lavish updo. Made in France from Italian acetate, it’s a luxury piece she most certainly doesn’t have yet.

Five words: Soft, sleek, and machine-washable. A silk pajama top is a prime example of loungewear gone luxe.

These crisp-feeling, lightweight utility pants give the gift of effortless dressing. Available in a palette of classic neutral colors and rotating seasonal options, the relaxed shape and adjustable waistband of these cotton pull-ons make them an easy pick as a weekend staple. They’re also blessedly machine-washable—and she’s probably going to reach for them as soon as the dryer cycle ends.

This necklace-scarf hybrid can instantly upgrade any white button-down or basic black cocktail dress. The natural silk cord rests comfortably on the skin, and the kelp pendant proviess an ethereal touch that is elegant but slightly bohemian.

If you noticed her binging Love Story or pinning various CBK-inspired styles (that’s Caroline Bessett-Kennedy to you, gentlemen), this rollneck from J.Crew made the rounds on TikTok, Instagram, Substack, and beyond for its 90s-nostalgia look. It’s, at the very least, a sweatshirt upgrade.

This It-girl jewelry piece from one of Gwyneth Paltrow’s favorite brands includes not one, not two, but three rings fashioned together with 18K gold hardware—so it’s kind of like getting multiple gifts in one. The mixed-metal appearance is great if you don’t know her preference between gold and silver, plus the versatile design lets her wear it across multiple fingers or stacked on one.

Lizzie Ames modeled this sterling silver band on a strip of filet lace, down to the open grid pattern and the scalloped edges. It’s made by hand in her Brooklyn studio and comes in at a generous 11 millimeters wide, so it stands on its own without a stack. It evokes a curated style that’s a little bit grandmother’s linen closet and a little bit art school.

The bigger the bow, the better. This silken black bag from playful brand Damson Madder is perfect for anyone who considers herself a loud but intentional dresser.

Ezcaray makes remarkable throw blankets, all hand-woven in mohair, but it’s sadly not socially acceptable to stay wrapped in one outside the home. Instead, buy her the miniature version: a plush scarf in a watercolor-like color palette to keep her warm all season long.

Cashmere sweaters are an obvious gifting move, but these gloves use the material in a surprising way. With the cashmere on the inside, under Italian-made suede, she’ll use them every day until April. The yellow-beige color is a great statement for under any of her big winter coats.

Erin Pollard started Underwater Weaving Studio partly because she found most basket-weaving kits dated and hard on beginner hands. This one comes with the materials and step-by-step instructions for a sturdy tote with two handles. So, after years of canvas tote bags, she gets a new hobby for the winter and a market bag she made herself by the summer. As unique gifts for women go, a weekend project beats another candle.

Here’s a journal that will actually motivate her to jot down her doctor’s appointments and after-work events lineup. She’ll have a hard time misplacing the notebook, thanks to the vibrant shade of blue, and you can add a personal touch with a thoughtful monogram or a horoscope emblem to pay homage to her birth month.

For the gal who has it all, a designer comb can travel with her anywhere—whether she’s jet-setting across the globe or just needs a touch-up between lunch and an afternoon work meeting.

She might have a lot of journals already, but she likely doesn’t have one that’s bound in ostrich-embossed Italian leather. The insert is refillable, so she can swap the pages once its weight or size gets unwieldy. Mémoire will hand-inscribe her initials, and it arrives in the brand’s keepsake packaging with a gift note included, which spares you an extra trip to the card aisle.

The clip gives us the clearest look yet at the Cosmos’ lighting, front and rear, after months of camouflaged prototype sightings. But the car itself is still about a year away.

Lucid posted the 1 minute 34 second video on X yesterday. The caption talks about “elevating the experience of movement” and says Lucid can’t wait “to share this feeling with even more people.” It doesn’t name the vehicle, but “even more people” is about as subtle a hint at a cheaper model as you can get.

Two frames from the film show the vehicle at dusk. At the rear, “LUCID” is spelled out in red illuminated letters across the tailgate, flanked by thin red light strips, with a spoiler cutting across the base of the rear glass. Up front, a sculpted LED headlight with a row of vertical segments sweeps across a red body panel.

That rear end matches the Cosmos design Lucid registered with the EU Intellectual Property Office in May, which showed the same spelled-out “LUCID” tailgate and rear-glass spoiler. It also lines up with the thin red light strips on the camouflaged Cosmos prototype spotted on Highway 101 in California last month.

Lucid unveiled its plans for Cosmos and Earth at its first Investor Day in March. Both ride on the new midsize platform and start under $50,000, roughly half the price of the Gravity.

On paper, the Cosmos is impressive. Lucid claims about 300 miles of range from a 69 kWh pack, thanks to efficiency of up to 4.5 mi/kWh, which it says is 10% better than its closest competitor. It also claims 200 miles of range in 14 minutes of charging, and its new Atlas drive unit has 30% fewer parts and costs 37% less than the Zeus unit in the Gravity.

The problem is timing. Production was supposed to start in late 2026. In August, CEO Silvio Napoli pushed the Cosmos to 2027, “most likely the second half.”

That puts it on the same schedule as Rivian’s $45,000 base R2, and well after the Tesla Model Y it was caught testing next to in Arizona back in May.

Lucid needs this car badly. It delivered 3,806 vehicles in Q3, down 7% year-over-year, while building only 2,954 after cutting the second shift at its Arizona factory.

I want Lucid to succeed. Period. I love the Air Pure and would like to get one at some point, but the cost is out of my budget while the tech is more than I want or need.

But I think what impresses me more than anything with Lucid is that they are one of the few who actually speak efficiency. It seems that they actually care about being efficient where companies like GM and others just build vehicles with bigger batteries in order to get more range. So for that, I give Lucid much credit.

The company is building hype a year out. It has nothing else new to sell until the Cosmos arrives, and the company reports Q3 earnings on Monday. They need to remind everyone what they are working toward.

A midsize SUV doing 4.5 mi/kWh would be best in class by a wide margin, and Lucid’s efficiency claims have held up on the Air. If it really lands under $50,000 with 300 miles of range, it’s a very compelling alternative to the Model Y and the R2, which still have room to take over market shares from ICE vehicles.

But Lucid has already slipped this car once; it says its cash lasts “well into 2027,” and the Cosmos is due in the second half of 2027. That’s a tight overlap. I think the Cosmos will be a good car, but can Lucid fund it all the way to customers’ driveways?

#4745. Tesla hikes Cybertruck prices up to 10% after announcing it will kill production

Tesla has raised Cybertruck prices in the US by up to 10% and stopped taking orders for the base Dual Motor AWD trim. The cheapest Cybertruck you can actually order now costs $92,490.

The move comes right after Tesla confirmed it will end Cybertruck production at Gigafactory Texas around mid-2027.

Here’s what Tesla’s online configurator shows today, compared to the prices set in August:

The Dual Motor trim still shows a new, higher price on Tesla’s website, but the option is greyed out. So Tesla raised the price of a version it isn’t selling anymore.

This is the second price hike in less than three months. Tesla raised prices by $5,000 on two trims in August, when the Dual Motor went from $69,990 to $74,990 and the Premium AWD from $79,990 to $84,990.

Add it up and the Premium AWD is now $12,500 (15.6%) more expensive than it was in early August. And the entry price for any Cybertruck you can order went from $69,990 to $92,490. That’s a 32% jump in about 10 weeks.

For reference, Tesla unveiled the Cybertruck in 2019 with a promised starting price of $39,900.

The price hikes make little sense from a demand standpoint. Tesla doesn’t break out Cybertruck deliveries, but its “Other Models” category, which also includes the Model S, Model X, and Semi, fell 48% year-over-year to 8,295 units in Q3. We estimate Cybertrucks made up 7,000 to 8,000 of those, about 12% of the line’s 250,000-unit annual capacity.

Tesla also tried the opposite approach earlier this year. It offered a dual-motor Cybertruck at $59,990 in February for “only the next 10 days,” then pulled it. A single-motor RWD version was discontinued after just 173 sales. None of it moved the needle.

The Cybertruck isn’t sold in Europe or most right-hand-drive markets, and Tesla canceled it for Australia and New Zealand last month.

So, Tesla has now discontinued more models than it currently offers. Looks like the great leader isn’t particularly good at writing product specs. And the hype has been over for quite a while anyway. In Europe, owning a Tesla has actually become something of an image liability.

This is what a wind-down looks like. Tesla isn’t trying to sell more Cybertrucks anymore. It’s trying to make as much money as possible on the last ones, with the hope that announcing the end of production will encourage some people to secure their order.

Once you’ve decided to end a program, volume stops mattering. You have a set number of build slots left, a parts supply you want to burn down, and probably a small group of fans who’ll want one before it’s gone. Pausing the cheapest trim and charging $7,500 more for the rest is the obvious play. You push everyone into higher-margin configurations and stop pretending the base truck is a real product.

But it does say a lot about the last two years of Cybertruck pricing. Tesla went from a $59,990 “limited-time” offer in February to a $92,490 entry price in November. That’s a company that never figured out who the truck was for.

#4741. Kia’s PV7 electric van stretches over 17 feet and seats 9

Kia is expanding its electric van lineup with the PV7, a larger PV5 sibling that can carry nine people or a whole lot of cargo.

The PV5, Kia’s first fully electric van from its Platform Beyond Vehicle (PBV) business, is proving to be a bigger hit than expected.

A year after it went on sale, the PV5 quickly became Europe’s most popular small electric van. In the first half of 2026, it was the top seller in its segment, accounting for 37% of electric C-segment van sales across Europe.

Next year, Kia will launch the PV7, the second electric van from its PBV business. Kia revealed the PV7 at IAA Transportation in Hanover, Germany, in September.

It’s based on the same E-GMP.S platform as the PV5, but the PV7 features a considerably longer wheelbase and stretched body, opening up more space inside.

The PV7 is over 17.5 ft long, measuring 5,350 mm long, 1,995 mm wide, and 1,990 mm high, with a 3,500 mm wheelbase. In comparison, the PV5 is just 4,695 mm long, 1,895 mm wide, and 1,915 mm tall, with a 2,995 mm wheelbase.

That’s even bigger than the Volkswagen ID. Buzz Long-Wheelbase (LWB), which measures 4,962 mm in length with a 3,239 mm wheelbase.

Like the PV5, the PV7 will initially be available in Passenger and Cargo body styles, but Kia plans to launch 23 different variants, or “top hats,” over the next few years.

It will be offered with two nickel-cobalt-manganese (NCM) battery packs: 71.5 kWh and 96.2 kWh. The Long Range Cargo model offers an all-electric WLTP range of over 460 km (285 miles). Even at full capacity, Kia said the new PV7 achieves nearly 400 km (248 miles) of range and still has 350 liters of trunk space.

A plena capacidad la nueva #PV7 consigue casi 400 km de autonomía y aún reserva 350 litros de maletero #Kia #KiaPV7 #MovementThatInspires pic.twitter.com/fzIvviYZuE

Front-wheel drive (FWD) will be standard at launch, but Kia plans to add an all-wheel drive (AWD) option later.

Depending on the configuration, the FWD electric powertrain delivers up to 268 horsepower (200 kW) and 309 lb-ft (420 Nm) of torque.

Thanks to its 800V architecture, the Kia PV7’s battery can charge from 10% to 80% in about 25 minutes with a 350 kW DC fast charger. It will be Kia’s first vehicle with two charging ports, including a front AC/DC port and an optional rear side AC port.

With vehicle-to-load (V2L) capabilities, it can serve as a mobile power source for tools, equipment, a campsite, or other external electronic devices.

The PV7 Cargo, designed for businesses, fleets, and logistics, is available in 2- and 3-seat configurations and offers up to 6.1 cubic meters of cargo space. The High Roof variant offers even more, with up to 8 cubic meters.

Maximum payload is up to 1,165 kg (2,568 lbs) for the Cargo Long and up to 1,200 kg (2,645 lbs) for the compact model.

The PV7 Cargo Long features a 550 mm loading height and, according to Kia, enough capacity for up to three Euro pallets (800 x 1,200 mm). An added heavy-duty mode adjusts the vehicle’s response to varying payloads to help maintain stability and control while driving.

Depending on the use, buyers can choose between full-open twin-swing tailgate doors or a lift-up tailgate.

The PV7 Passenger, on the other hand, is designed for personal use and families, or can also be used as a shuttle with room for up to nine passengers in the global version. In Korea, it will seat up to 11 passengers.

The 7-seater features Long-Rail Easy Remove Seats, enabling various interior seating configurations. The 9-seater variant, on the other hand, is available with or without a fourth row.

Inside, both versions feature Hyundai’s new Pleos Connect infotainment system, with 12.9″ and 14.6″ display screens and physical controls for commonly used functions.

The system runs Android Automotive OS, making it more like a smartphone with apps and customizable screens. It also includes Hyundai’s Gleo AI, an AI-powered in-car companion that can answer questions, control navigation or vehicle functions, and more.

Nice vehicle but once again Kia/Hyundai short changes on battery capacity. A 138" (3500 mm) wheelbase means plenty of room for a 140-150kwh battery (BMW and Rivian do that with vastly less space). That would give it a proper EPA range of over 300 miles with passengers or cargo. Instead this will be in the low 200s unloaded and 170-190 IRL. Offer it as a $7k upgrade. smh

Kia said the PV7 is based on a “Mobile Workspace” concept, with a layered dashboard and center console to optimize space.

The Kia PV7 Passenger and Cargo will go on sale in Korea and Europe in the second half of 2027. It will then roll out to new markets with new derivatives and conversions.

Kia will announce PV7 prices closer to its launch. In Korea, the PV5 Passenger and Cargo Compact starts at 45.9 million won ($34,000) and 41 million won ($30,000), respectively. In Germany, the PV5 Passenger 5-seater starts at €38,690 ($43,000).

#4739. The Next Generation of Weight-Loss Drugs Is Reshaping People’s Looks—And Not in a Flattering Way

WHEN YOU LOSE weight through traditional diet and exercise, you tend to see a gradual slimming down of your face. But when you add in gray-market peptides like retatrutide, you’re expediting the weight loss process. That also includes rapid fat loss in the face, leaving a sunken and hollowed-out look people are dubbing “reta face.”

Online Reddit communities on peptides and biohacking are packed with people commenting on changes to their facial appearance after taking retatrutide—a triple hormone agonist of the GLP-1, GIP, and glucagon receptors that’s expected to become the next generation of weight-loss injections. One clinical trial found those taking retatrutide had more than double the weight loss of people taking Ozempic.

To be fair, “Ozempic face” has also been an issue. But with Eli Lilly expected to apply for FDA approval of retatrutide in early 2027 for obesity and other conditions, doctors say reta will likely cause more facial volume issues. Is there any way to prevent these unflattering side effects? We went straight to the doctors currently treating people with facial symptoms from GLPs.

WHILE RETA FACE isn’t an official medical diagnosis, it’s a real phenomenon. “The facial changes can be kind of dramatic,” says Mir Ali, MD, medical director of MemorialCare Surgical Weight Loss Center at Orange Coast Medical Center. But the lack of criteria has also caused some debate over what qualifies as reta face.

On the r/BodyHackGuide community (with over 87,000 contributors dubbed “Lab Rats”), reta face before-and-after posts are recurring discussion threads. Some describe reta face as a chiseled look after weight loss while Ozempic face is the more sickly face. Others argue that “reta face” and “Ozempic face” are simply two terms to describe the sunken look from your face losing fat.

“Reta face is the new Ozempic face,” says dermatologist Gary Goldenberg, MD. “Since retatrutide is a triple biologic agonist that produces more significant weight loss than GLP peptides, patients may have an even more exaggerated appearance of a sunken, aged look.”

That means cheeks can become flat and hollow, temples narrow, and undereye areas can look sunken and dark. “Facial bones can also become more prominent as fat disappears,” says Dr. Goldenberg. “The skin can thin, as collagen and elastic fibers have less underlying fat plumping them up.”

Joshua Zeichner, MD, director of cosmetic and clinical research in dermatology at Mount Sinai Hospital, says the shape of your face changes with any significant weight loss—it’s just more apparent when someone is on a weight-loss medication.

ABSOLUTELY. DR. ZEICHNER says minimizing the appearance of facial wasting is all about losing weight slowly—even when taking a GLP-1 or reta. While you can’t target specific areas for fat loss, Dr. Goldenberg recommends pacing yourself while still getting plenty of protein on your plate and being selective about meals that have enough nutrients.

If you already have reta face and the appearance bothers you, Dr. Goldenberg recommends seeing a dermatologist. “Collagen stimulators and fillers are a very common treatment for this problem,” he says. “Volume can be restored and contouring can be improved with these treatments.”

#4738. The BMW iX3 smashed its EPA range rating, driving well over 400 miles in a real-world test

BMW’s new iX3 outperformed the Volvo EX60 and Mercedes-Benz GLC EV, driving well over 400 miles during a real-world range test.

In a recent nationally representative survey, BMW found that Americans want more EV range than they actually need.

The study found that 73% consider 75 miles of range, or less, enough to cover their daily driving. Meanwhile, 42% said they would require at least 300 miles of range to consider an EV.

Another 53% said they would be more likely to consider an EV if it could add about 150 miles of range in 10 minutes.

BMW’s new iX3 checks all the boxes. Based on BMW’s sixth-generation (Gen6) eDrive 800V system, the 2027 iX3 50 xDrive delivers an EPA-estimated range of up to 434 miles (with 20″ summer tires).

With the 22″ summer tires, the iX3 50 xDrive has an EPA-estimated range of up to 392 miles. Still, plenty for at least a week of commuting.

It can also add 170-185 miles of range in 10 minutes with up to 400 kW DC fast charging. In everyday, real-world driving, it may drive even further than its official EPA numbers suggest.

During Edmunds‘ EV Range test, the 2027 BMW iX3 50 xDrive (with 22″ summer tires) drove 436 miles on a single charge, topping its EPA estimate of 392 miles by 44 miles.

The electric SUV was also more efficient than advertised. The iX3 achieved an energy consumption of 28.3 kWh per 100 miles, beating its EPA estimate of 32 kWh per 100 miles by roughly 11.6%.

BMW’s new iX3 is now the longest-range luxury electric SUV that Edmunds has tested, outperforming rivals including the 2027 Volvo EX60 (352 miles) and Mercedes-Benz GLC Electric (392 miles).

The Edmunds real-world range test is designed to provide a more accurate estimate of an EV’s range in everyday driving conditions.

It consists of 60% city and 40% highway driving with an average speed of 40 mph. The vehicle stays within 5 mph of the posted speed limit, and the climate control is set to auto at 72 degrees.

The 2027 BMW iX3 50 xDrive is available to order in Sport, M Sport, and M Sport Professional trims, priced from $61,500, $64,000, and $65,500, respectively.

Average speed of 40 mph in perfect weather is an absolute best case scenario for EVs. I think cold weather 70 mph would be the worst case and it should be tested.

That said, I think BMW and Mercedes tend to underrate their cars published range (I think they publish worst case condition range). BMW iX and Mercedes have historically outperformed EPA ratings according to various articles and reddits posts.

But I think regardless of what we think of Edmunds tests, these are some crazy range figures and with roughly 100kwh usable battery capacity, you are still looking at close to 4 miles per kwh. As an example across the Ultium platform anything from Chevy or Cadillac barely breaches 300 miles. The big Escalade and pickup trucks have 225+ kwh battery so I am not counting them.

If the depreciation rate for luxury EVs holds up, in 2-3 years, they will be awesome value.

Powered by a 108.7 kWh battery, the new iX3 with 20″ Summer Tires delivers up to 434 miles of range on a single charge.

With a charging rate of up to 400 kW, the new BMW iX3 can recharge from 10% to 80% in about 21 minutes, or add about 185 miles in 10 minutes.

Inside, the electric SUV features the Neue Klasse interior design. The setup includes BMW’s new Panoramic Vision, a full-length windshield display, and a 17.9″ central infotainment screen running the latest Operating System X. Buyers can also upgrade to the optional BMW 3D Head-Up Display.
